36.Option: Stratifying the analysis by gestational age at delivery to examine differences in temperature associations across preterm birth subtypes

36.Rationale: The passage explicitly warns that stratifying by gestational age can induce collider bias and therefore is not the preferred approach for examining differences by PTB timing. The authors instead used an extension of the Cox model with time-dependent coefficients 'without stratifying the model' to avoid that bias. Evidence: We fitted Cox proportional-hazards models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM [ 28 , 40 ].

Z i ( t ) represents time-dependent covariates (sine and cosine of the week of the year for each gestation week, adjusting for seasonality), and X i represents the time-dependent exposures (i.e. weekly temperature) added into the model in a cross-basis function s x ( X i , t ; β x ).

Combining a Cox model with time-dependent covariates and a DLNM allows modeling temporally varying exposures and their lagged effects while the sine/cosine seasonality terms adjust for seasonal confounding that changes over time. This directly addresses confounders that vary over gestation and the exposure–outcome time dynamics, thereby best matching the question.

A study in Sweden defined exposure weeks backward from the week of birth, which leads to a similar limitation [ 30 ].
Our exposures were defined by gestation week, while theirs were determined by the date of birth, which does not correspond to a specific gestation week.
36.Rationale: The passage criticizes approaches that define exposure windows relative to birth date (calendar weeks backward from birth) because they mix reference times and limit interpretation of critical gestational windows. Fixed calendar-week windows relative to birth do not appropriately account for varying gestational lengths and time-varying confounding in the way the authors' gestation-week-based DLNM with time-dependent Cox does, so this option is not the best feature for minimizing the described bias.

Evidence: Other cohort studies have examined longer-term exposures, such as the last month before birth, the entire pregnancy average, and trimester-specific exposures [ 19–26 ]. While our results partly overlap with those of these studies, it is challenging to draw comparisons due to the different exposure windows. More importantly, these studies examined each exposure window in a separate model, raising concern that some associations were confounded by exposure in other gestation weeks.
36.Rationale: Fitting separate (time-fixed) models by trimester was criticized in the passage because correlated temperatures across periods can confound associations between windows. A time-fixed Cox with separate trimester analyses would not adequately handle time-varying confounding or the lagged structure of exposure, so it does not minimize the bias described and is therefore incorrect.

Evidence: DLNMs can also estimate associations of cumulative exposures throughout pregnancy, calculated for scenarios of fixed exposure relative to another fixed reference exposure. Evidence: We conducted interrupted time series (ITS) analysis by using monthly counts of outpatient department visits for selected NCDs (CVD, CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD) to evaluate the impacts of lockdown on health service utilization after controlling for time-invariant confounders, seasonality, and long-term trend affecting the population-level distribution of these diseases [ 16 , 17 ].

Evidence: We controlled the models for seasonality by using Fourier terms, incorporated an indicator variable for the time to control long-term effect, and included a 1-month lag of residuals in the model to control residual autocorrelation.

56.Option: Including polygenic risk scores as covariates in regression models to adjust for genetic confounding
Evidence: Previous studies on child maltreatment have used, e.g. twin designs [ 25 ] and Mendelian randomization [ 26 ] to adjust for unobserved familial confounding, whereas studies on household dysfunction indicators, such as parental divorce or mental health problems, have addressed this issue using, e.g. children-of-twins and adoption designs [ 27–30 ], or molecular genetics designs, such as polygenic risk scores together with single nucleotide polymorphism based heritability [ 22 , 30 ].

57.Option: The application of a negative control outcome analysis confirms that the observed increase in incidence is specific to the screening population and not due to broader secular trends
Evidence: First, we performed the negative control outcome analysis by repeating the SCM among people aged 35–39, who did not undergo screening. Demonstrating good predictive fit before the intervention is a key methodological feature that increases confidence that post-intervention divergences reflect the intervention rather than pre-existing differences or model misspecification.

57.Option: The use of a flexible SCM approach that relaxes the convex hull condition enables the synthetic control to extrapolate beyond observed data, allowing for more accurate detection of intervention effects

Thus the statement as phrased is not supported as the central methodological feature ensuring attribution.

Thus, any observed differences after the implementation start can be reasonably ascribed to the intervention.
57.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that SCM constructs a weighted synthetic control to match pre-intervention incidence trajectories and that when pre-intervention trajectories are similar, post-intervention divergences can be reasonably ascribed to the intervention. Matching pre-intervention trends in a counterfactual control group is therefore the core methodological feature that supports attributing observed changes to the screening program rather than pre-existing trends or external factors.

Evidence: Covariates for all analyses included child sex, maternal age at delivery, maternal education, or marital status as indicators for prenatal socioeconomic status, and maternal pre-pregnancy overweight or obesity status. 58.Rationale: While a stronger methylation signal among infants with family history could indicate gene–environment interplay, it would not by itself distinguish biologically causal epigenetic effects from confounding by inherited genetic variation or shared familial environment. The passage notes maternal history of asthma was treated as a covariate, but it does not present evidence that methylation differences were more pronounced by family history. Therefore this option does not provide the clearest support that methylation is biologically relevant (it could reflect genetic confounding), so it is not a strong independent indicator in this study context.

Evidence: Childhood asthma is thought to arise from immune dysregulation [ 3 ]. DNAm present in blood at birth may reflect early-life immunological disturbances that may contribute to asthma development later in childhood.

58.Rationale: Prospective association between newborn methylation and later asthma diagnosis indicates that methylation precedes disease and is predictive of future asthma, which supports biological relevance rather than being a cross-sectional correlate of population structure. Evidence: In race-stratified analysis, we examined the direction and magnitude of effect in a subset of 27 CpGs ( Supplementary Table S4 ) between newborns who later developed asthma and those who did not across self- reported race groups. Among the top ranked 27 CpGs that we examined, most (70%) showed a consistent effect across self-reported black and white race groups. 58.Rationale: Consistency of methylation–asthma associations across racial and ethnic groups reduces the likelihood that findings are due to population stratification or ancestry-specific variation. Replicable effects across diverse subpopulations strengthen the case that the methylation differences reflect biology relevant to asthma pathogenesis rather than only population-level differences.

Models 2a–c had individual education added to Models 1a–c to test whether these associations held after adjusting for individual SEP.

The authors explicitly describe testing as a potential confounder and use separate methods (age-stratified testing data and adjustment) to address it, so timing stratification alone is not the most direct methodological choice to handle testing-related reporting bias.

Evidence: Although systematic nationwide data on testing by age group do not exist, we obtained data from four jurisdictions on age-stratified COVID-19 testing rates.
Using these data we examine whether testing rates rose in children after schools opened, and then adjust the regression estimates to account for differential rates of testing.

Fig. 5 shows reported cases of COVID-19 in children adjusted for testing rates with a blue dashed line. 60.Rationale: The passage states that the investigators obtained age-stratified testing data from four jurisdictions and explicitly adjusted regression estimates for differential testing rates. Evidence: Third, wastewater analysis from 2022 also suggests that school openings had little to no relationship with case rates across the USA [ 33 ].

60.Rationale: Wastewater surveillance is cited as supplementary corroborative evidence that school openings had little relationship with case rates. However, it is not the primary methodological choice the investigators used to address the specific problem of testing-driven reporting bias. The study's main, direct approach to that problem was obtaining age-stratified testing data and adjusting case estimates accordingly; wastewater data served as an additional line of evidence rather than the central methodological control for testing behavior.

Evidence: Note that, as all schools reopened for in-person learning in the Fall of 2021, there is no control group of schools that did not open. An important potential confounder is that the COVID-19 testing threshold among children may be correlated with school opening due to public health measures.
60.Rationale: The authors used an event-study (timing-based) design rather than a difference-in-differences comparing open vs closed schools, because all schools reopened. They did control for mask mandates as a covariate, but comparing counties by mask policy would not directly isolate testing behavior and, per the passage, a diff-in-diff across school opening status was not appropriate. The primary method to address testing-related bias was adjustment using age-stratified testing data, not a mask-mandate diff-in-diff.

Evidence: For example, using maternal genotype to proxy offspring genetic variants related to birthweight would also likely include variants that pleiotropically influence maternal blood pressure and glucose levels.

However, it relies on a number of assumptions that have previously been discussed at length [ 12 , 13 ] ( Fig. 1a and Supplementary Material).
61.Rationale: Using maternal genotypes as instruments does not mitigate confounding by the maternal genome; the passage explicitly warns that maternal genotype used to proxy offspring genotype would likely include variants that pleiotropically influence maternal outcomes (thus violating the independence/exclusion assumptions). Therefore this design would not effectively mitigate maternal genotype confounding.

61.Option: Mendelian randomization using offspring genotypes from linked health records in spousal pairs
Evidence: However, these approaches are difficult to perform at scale because of the paucity of genotyped parent–offspring dyads and trios across the world’s cohorts [ 16 ].
Consequently, this limits the utility and broader application of MR in investigating the causal effect of offspring perinatal traits on maternal health outcomes.
61.Rationale: Using offspring genotypes would avoid maternal genotype confounding if properly implemented, but it requires genotyped offspring (mother–offspring dyads or trios). The passage emphasizes that such approaches are difficult to perform at scale due to a paucity of genotyped parent–offspring data, so they do not meet the criterion of enabling analysis in large, population-based cohorts without genotyped offspring.

61.Option: Offspring genotype-by-proxy Mendelian randomization using paternal genotypes
Evidence: The offspring genotype-by-proxy MR approach enables MR studies of the causal effect of offspring perinatal traits on their mother’s outcomes when offspring genotypes are not available, but paternal genotypes are.

We utilize the paternal genotype to proxy the offspring genotype, which should be uncorrelated with maternal genotype in the absence of assortative mating and therefore protect MR analyses from confounding by the maternal genome.

Given the increasing availability of datasets such as the UK Biobank that (incidentally) include tens of thousands of genome-wide genotyped spousal pairs [ 18 ], the offspring genotype-by-proxy MR approach could augment causal analyses of perinatal offspring exposures on their mother’s outcomes.
61.Rationale: The passage explicitly describes offspring genotype-by-proxy MR using paternal genotypes as an approach that (1) works when offspring genotypes are not available, (2) uses paternal genotype to proxy offspring genotype and thereby minimizes confounding by maternal genotype (absent assortative mating), and (3) is feasible in large population datasets because many biobanks (e.g., UK Biobank) include tens of thousands of genotyped spousal pairs. Thus this design best matches the question requirements.

61.Option: Mendelian randomization with adjustment for maternal genotype in mother–offspring dyads
Evidence: Conditioning on maternal genotype (i.e. at the same loci as in the offspring; as indicated in Fig. 1b ) is one way to block this path of maternal confounding [ 12 ]. We refer to this approach as “MR with adjustment for maternal genotype.”

In contrast, both MR conditional on maternal genotype and MR using paternally transmitted alleles require genotyped mother–offspring or father–offspring dyads, even when implemented in the two-sample design ( Table 1 ).
However, these approaches are difficult to perform at scale because of the paucity of genotyped parent–offspring dyads and trios across the world’s cohorts [ 16 ].
61.Rationale: While MR with adjustment for maternal genotype does mitigate maternal genotype confounding by conditioning on maternal genotype, it requires genotyped mother–offspring dyads. The passage notes such dyads are scarce and therefore this approach is not well suited to large population-based cohorts that lack genotyped offspring, so it does not meet the question constraint.

61.Option: Mendelian randomization using paternally transmitted alleles in genotyped parent–offspring trios
Evidence: Alternatively, the availability of genomic data on parent–offspring trios and/or mother–offspring dyads permits the identification of paternally transmitted alleles, which should also avoid confounding by the maternal genome ( Fig. 1c ; referred to as “MR using paternally transmitted alleles”) [ 14 ].
However, these approaches are difficult to perform at scale because of the paucity of genotyped parent–offspring dyads and trios across the world’s cohorts [ 16 ].

In comparison, pleiotropy through the paternal genome resulted in biased causal estimates in all approaches, with the magnitude of bias largest in the offspring by proxy MR approach, followed by the paternal transmitted haplotype approach.
61.Rationale: Using paternally transmitted alleles can reduce maternal genotype confounding and has less bias from paternal pleiotropy than the proxy approach, but it requires genotyped parent–offspring trios/dyads. The passage states such genotyped trios are scarce and thus this design cannot easily enable analyses in large population-based cohorts without genotyped offspring, which was a requirement in the question.

Evidence: In malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa, a large proportion of acute febrile illnesses in children are caused by malaria or pneumonia.

it is thought that metabolic acidosis, which is common in malaria patients and often compensated for by deep breathing, could provide an explanation [ 6 ].

Evidence: The most important associations with CXR-positivity were, in rank order: lower chest wall indrawing [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) =18.1, 95% confidence interval (95% CI): 1.9, 175.8, P = 0.012], crackles on chest auscultation (aOR = 13.1, 95% CI: 1.4, 127.4, P = 0.027), and nasal flaring (aOR = 5.9, 95% CI: 1.1, 32.8, P = 0.041). malaria infection is common in the region [ 17 ] and frequently associated with respiratory symptoms [ 12 , 18 , 19 ].

Evidence: Among 1650 cases had both a CXR result and a malaria result, with 798 (48.4%) exhibiting radiological signs of pneumonia and 77 (4.7%) testing positive for malaria parasitaemia.

62.Rationale: The passage supports that in malaria-endemic settings a substantial fraction of WHO-defined pneumonia cases can be misclassified and that many malaria-associated WHO pneumonia cases are CXR-negative (i.e., a normal chest X-ray is consistent with misclassification). Evidence: In malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa, a large proportion of acute febrile illnesses in children are caused by malaria or pneumonia.
malaria infection is common in the region [ 17 ] and frequently associated with respiratory symptoms [ 12 , 18 , 19 ].
it is thought that metabolic acidosis, which is common in malaria patients and often compensated for by deep breathing, could provide an explanation [ 6 ].
62.Rationale: The passage indicates that malaria frequently produces respiratory symptoms (for example via metabolic acidosis leading to deep breathing), so one would not expect a 'normal respiratory rate and no signs of respiratory distress' as a characteristic replacement of pneumonia signs. The most important associations with CXR-positivity were, in rank order: lower chest wall indrawing ... crackles on chest auscultation ... and nasal flaring ...

Prolonged cough and 'bilateral lung sounds' implying a viral respiratory infection are not described as a pattern distinguishing malaria from pneumonia in the provided data, so this option is unsupported.

It further suggests differential misclassification could lead to over-estimation of COVID-19 deaths among some high-education Hispanic groups, which is the opposite of the scenario proposed. Thus the option's specific claim (underreporting among high-education people causing inflated disparities) is not supported by the text.

Evidence: This framework was evident in the context of COVID-19 in the US, exemplified by: ... (3) Social, political, and environmental factors: unequal health insurance coverage left 28 million US citizens uninsured or underinsured in 2020 [ 24 ], disproportionately affecting socioeconomically deprived populations and racial and ethnic minorities [ 25 ].

Evidence: racial and ethnic minorities (except Hispanics) have higher odds of hypertension [ 18 ] while behavioral risk factors like smoking and obesity are more common among individuals with a low SES [ 19–21 ]. Type 2 diabetes prevalence and mortality follow a socioeconomic gradient [ 20 , 22 ].
preexisting conditions like diabetes and hypertension were linked to increased risks of severe COVID-19 disease and mortality [ 23 ].

diseases of the heart alone were related to losses of −0.5 to −0.6 years (12%–14%) among Black men with low and middle education and Black women with low education.
63.Rationale: The passage documents higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes and other NCDs along socioeconomic gradients and states that these preexisting conditions increase risk of severe COVID-19. It further shows substantial LE losses from cardiovascular disease and other NCDs concentrated among low-education and Black subgroups. Therefore higher chronic disease burden in low-education populations plausibly contributed to both greater COVID severity and non-COVID mortality, explaining part of the disparity in LE losses.

Evidence: behavioral risk factors like smoking and obesity are more common among individuals with a low SES [ 19–21 ].
Adverse interactions: smoking and obesity exacerbate the course of a COVID-19 infection [ 23 ]
Nineteen COD categories were selected to include ... deaths of despair (including alcohol use disorder, alcohol and opioid poisoning, suicide, liver disease, and cirrhosis).

In 2020, some of the largest LE losses from non-COVID-19 causes were due to NCDs ... Unintentional injuries also contributed large LE losses ... Low-education White women lost −0.4 years (15%) due to deaths of despair.
63.Rationale: The passage states obesity is more common in low-SES populations and that obesity exacerbates COVID-19 severity. It also includes liver disease among causes (deaths of despair) contributing to LE losses and documents substantial non-COVID mortality among low-education groups. 64.Option: Chronic stress and inflammation resulting from neighborhood-level environmental and social conditions
Evidence: The biological underpinnings for the association of where people live with MM incidence are hypothesized to be rooted in stress and inflammation pathways.

Neighborhoods characterized by concentrated disadvantage and low SES are sources of chronic stress, given the limited resources, high crime rates and perceived threats to safety, limited transportation available, crowding, and noise exposure [ 40 , 41 ].
Chronic inflammation and inflammatory diseases have been linked to MM incidence [ 38 , 39 ].

It also describes how concentrated disadvantage is a source of chronic stress (quotation 2) and cites links between chronic inflammation and MM (quotation 3). Evidence: Participants who lived in areas with the highest concentrated disadvantage were more likely to be obese (36% vs 22%), smoke cigarettes (21% vs 11%), and reside in the Northeast region (34% vs 24%) of the USA and less likely to have graduated from college (32% vs 58%) and to engage in physical activity (55% vs 65%) compared with those in areas of lowest disadvantage.

Women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage had a 51% increase in the incidence of MM (Quartile 4 vs Quartile 1, HR: 1.51, 95% CI: 1.06, 2.15, P trend: .002 and HR: 1.48, 95% CI: 1.02, 2.13, P trend: .003) in age-adjusted and MV-adjusted analyses, respectively (the change in estimates was primarily affected by the inclusion of BMI in the MV models).
64.Rationale: Although smoking prevalence was higher in disadvantaged neighborhoods (quotation 1), alcohol did not differ (quotation 2), and crucially, the multivariable models adjusted for smoking and alcohol (quotation 3). The association remained after adjustment (quotation 4), indicating differences in smoking or alcohol consumption do not fully explain the observed neighborhood effect. Thus this option is not the most likely sole explanation.

64.Option: Reduced access to preventive care and early cancer screening in neighborhoods of concentrated disadvantage
Evidence: residents of lower-resourced neighborhoods may experience limited access to high-quality preventive care [ 21 ] and barriers to safe recreation [ 22 ].

We identified incident cases of MM through self-reports on biennial questionnaires, linkages with state cancer registries in states in which >95% of the BWHS participants live, and linkages with the National Death Index [ 35 ]. Self-reported MM diagnoses were confirmed by a review of medical records, pathology reports, and cancer registry records.
In this large, prospective cohort of Black women living in the USA, we found that women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage were at a higher risk of MM regardless of educational attainment.
We controlled for several potential confounders; however, we did not have any information on family history of MM.
64.Rationale: The passage notes limited access to preventive care as a neighborhood disadvantage (quotation 1). However, MM is typically ascertained via cancer registries and validated medical records in this cohort (quotation 2), reducing the likelihood that differential screening alone produced the observed association. The authors highlight biological mechanisms (stress/inflammation) more directly (see option 0) and report a persistent association after adjusting for covariates (quotation 3). Therefore, while reduced access to care could contribute to disparities in outcomes, it is less likely to be the primary explanation for the increased MM incidence observed here.

64.Option: Increased prevalence of obesity due to limited access to healthy food and safe spaces for physical activity in disadvantaged neighborhoods
Evidence: Obesity [ 7 ] and pesticides (usually via occupational exposure) [ 8–11 ] are the most consistent established modifiable risk factors for MM.
Participants who lived in areas with the highest concentrated disadvantage were more likely to be obese (36% vs 22%) ... compared with those in areas of lowest disadvantage.
Multivariable (MV) models were additionally adjusted for cumulative average BMI (<25, 25–29, 30–34, ≥35 kg/m 2 ), educational attainment ...

Women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage had a 51% increase in the incidence of MM ... in age-adjusted and MV-adjusted analyses, respectively (the change in estimates was primarily affected by the inclusion of BMI in the MV models).
64.Rationale: Obesity is an established risk factor for MM and is more prevalent in disadvantaged neighborhoods (quotations 1 and 2). The authors note that inclusion of BMI in multivariable models primarily affected the estimates (quotation 4), suggesting obesity partially mediates the neighborhood–MM relationship. However, the association persisted after adjustment for BMI (quotation 3), and the authors emphasize stress/inflammation as the hypothesized underlying mechanism. Therefore obesity likely contributes but is not the single most likely explanation for the residual association after accounting for individual-level SES.

65.Option: The intervention improved timeliness by increasing the number of health facility visits during the postnatal period, thereby enhancing caregiver engagement with the health system
Evidence: Text message reminders might improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration as they keep individuals aware of vaccination schedules.
Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home.
The intervention involved an interaction between lay CHWs, pregnant women, and healthcare workers using a mobile phone application linked to a central registry.
participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period.
65.Rationale: While the passage describes text message reminders that 'notify them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination,' it does not present direct evidence that the intervention increased the absolute number of postnatal facility visits or that greater caregiver engagement (beyond prompting) was the primary mechanism. The authors emphasize that the reminders keep caregivers aware and reach mobile individuals who are 'unlikely to be found at home,' suggesting the key function was improved communication to mobile populations rather than a documented increase in general postnatal clinic attendance. Therefore this option overstates a mechanism (increased facility visits) that is not directly demonstrated in the text.

65.Option: Text message reminders effectively compensated for structural barriers related to mobility and limited access by enabling timely communication with caregivers who are frequently absent from fixed locations
Evidence: Viwandani is composed of a mobile population [ 9 , 10 ], served by private health facilities and two public health facilities that provide free routine immunization services although both are located outside the area [ 5 ] and characterized by poor uptake of and access to health services, especially vaccination [ 11 , 12 ].
In-person reminders through lay community health workers (CHWs) are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers as they frequently change locations and are unavailable during routine work hours.
Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home.
We leveraged the widespread use of mobile phones and text reminders as a low-cost intervention to nudge parents toward timely vaccinations, ultimately increasing immunization rates.
participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period.
65.Rationale: The passage explicitly frames the problem as a 'mobile population' with 'poor uptake of and access to health services' and states that 'in-person reminders ... are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers.' It then states that 'text reminders ... will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home' and that the intervention used automated text reminders to prompt timely vaccination. These statements directly support the interpretation that the reminders compensated for mobility- and access-related barriers by enabling timely communication with caregivers, making this the most likely explanation for the observed improvement in timeliness.

65.Option: The observed improvement in timeliness was due to the intervention's ability to reduce parental anxiety about vaccine safety, leading to greater willingness to vaccinate their newborns
Evidence: notable factors contributing to delayed vaccination uptake included parental lack of information, difficult access to health facilities, lack of finance and parental support, and distrust in vaccines and vaccination programs [ 3 ];
Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home.
participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period.

Our trial showed a trend toward improved timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the intervention period compared to the control period. The intervention effect was relatively larger for both OPV and BCG (19%) than separately for OPV (16%) and BCG (14%).
65.Rationale: Although the passage notes 'distrust in vaccines and vaccination programs' as a background barrier, it does not present evidence that the text messages were designed to or actually reduced parental anxiety about vaccine safety. The described content and intent of the intervention focus on reminders ('notify them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination') and addressing forgetfulness and communication gaps, not on education to allay safety concerns. Therefore attributing the timeliness improvement primarily to reduced vaccine-safety anxiety is not supported by the text.

65.Option: The improvement in timeliness was primarily driven by the increased availability of vaccines at the health facilities during the intervention period, which reduced supply-side delays
Evidence: Both private and public health facilities free vaccine from the government provided they are accredited as a vaccination center. In Viwandani several private facilities are not accredited to vaccinate babies but two public facilities and a few private ones offer vaccinations.
Therefore, our findings suggest text message reminders could be combined with incentives and/or approaches to increase access to vaccination services to improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccines.
The pragmatic trial was conducted in a real-world setting as the usual service providers implemented the intervention.
65.Rationale: The passage does not report any change in vaccine supply or facility availability coinciding with the intervention period. Instead, it treats the intervention as a low-cost reminder system implemented within existing services ('usual service providers implemented the intervention') and even suggests combining reminders with measures that increase access in future studies. There is no evidence presented that supply-side improvements occurred during the intervention, so this explanation is not supported.

65.Option: The intervention's success was due to the use of lay community health workers (CHWs) who provided in-person follow-up, ensuring caregivers adhered to the vaccination schedule
Evidence: In-person reminders through lay community health workers (CHWs) are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers as they frequently change locations and are unavailable during routine work hours.
The intervention involved an interaction between lay CHWs, pregnant women, and healthcare workers using a mobile phone application linked to a central registry.

Two lay CHWs selected from each village were trained to register all pregnant women in their second or third trimester using a mobile phone. The lay CHWs captured demographic variables of the pregnant women... and relayed the data to a central database. This triggered automated reminder messages to pregnant women through their mobile phones, lay CHWs, family members, or a friend about when the women were expected to deliver.
At delivery, lay CHWs documented the date of delivery of the child and submitted the data to the central database.
65.Rationale: Although lay CHWs were involved in registration, documentation, and relaying data, the passage explicitly states that 'in-person reminders through lay community health workers (CHWs) are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers' in this mobile population. The described role of CHWs in this trial was to enable the text-message system (registration and data relay), not to conduct routine in-person follow-up to ensure adherence. Therefore attributing the observed effect primarily to in-person CHW follow-up contradicts the study description.

66.Option: Individuals in the North and Center-West regions, where health services are less developed, show the lowest vaccine coverage, indicating that access to healthcare infrastructure is the primary driver of vaccine uptake rather than public health messaging
Evidence: The Southeast region exhibited the highest vaccine coverage for both influenza and COVID-19, while the North and Center-West regions showed the lowest.

COVID-19 vaccine coverage varies among the country’s regions, being lower in municipalities with lower education levels, higher proportions of Afro descendants, high income, and worse health service indicators [ 17 ].
66.Rationale: While the passage documents lower coverage in the North and Center-West and links regional variation to worse health service indicators, it does not conclude that infrastructure/access rather than messaging or trust is the primary driver. The cited text shows geographic disparities exist but does not rule out messaging/trust effects; elsewhere the passage highlights cultural/religious messaging effects (e.g., evangelicals) that persisted after adjustment. Therefore the option's claim that access is the primary driver ("rather than public health messaging") is not supported by the passage.

66.Option: Indigenous individuals, who face higher clinical risk due to comorbidities and limited access to care, show the lowest vaccine uptake, indicating that systemic inequities in health access outweigh the influence of public health messaging and trust
Evidence: White subjects exhibited the highest COVID-19 vaccination rates, while Indigenous individuals showed the lowest.
We were unable to find any nationwide studies of vaccination rates among Indigenous individuals with which our results could have been compared.
66.Rationale: The passage confirms Indigenous individuals had the lowest coverage, but it does not assert that systemic inequities in access 'outweigh' messaging/trust. In fact, the manuscript emphasizes non-clinical influences on uptake (for example, religious affiliation and information/messaging). The evidence cited about Indigenous status documents low coverage but does not demonstrate that access is the dominant explanation over messaging or trust, so the option overstates what the data support.

66.Option: Individuals aged 0–19 years, who are at lower clinical risk for severe outcomes, show the lowest uptake of four or more COVID-19 doses, suggesting that public health messaging is more influential than clinical risk in shaping vaccine behavior
Evidence: COVID-19 coverage tended to increase with age, ranging from only 6.0% in those aged 0–19 years to >60% after the age of 60 years.

This reflects the prioritization of older adults in the initial stages of the vaccine rollout in 2020, when uptake in this group was higher than for any other age range, which was soon followed by a reduction in mortality after age 60 [ 27 ].
66.Rationale: Although the 0–19 age group had very low uptake, the passage attributes much of the age pattern to prioritization policies and differing perceived/actual clinical risk (older adults were prioritized and had higher uptake). Therefore low uptake among young people can be explained by clinical risk/prioritization rather than proving that messaging outweighs clinical risk. The evidence thus does not support the option's inference that messaging is the dominant influence.

66.Option: Evangelical individuals, despite varying clinical risk, show markedly lower vaccine uptake even after adjusting for socioeconomic and demographic factors, indicating that trust in health systems and messaging outweighs individual clinical risk
Evidence: Evangelicals had markedly lower coverage than the other religions ( P < 0.001) and the ratio to nonreligious individuals became even more marked in the adjusted (CR = 0.69) than in the unadjusted (CR = 0.86) analyses.

the findings that evangelicals are 16 pp less likely to be vaccinated against COVID-19 than Catholics is not surprising, and smaller studies in Brazil [ 32 ] and in England [ 33 ] pointed in the same direction.

Evangelicals as a group tend to be strongly supportive of right-wing political parties, including the one led by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who is a spoken anti-vaccine person who states that he was never vaccinated [ 30 , 31 ].

lower vaccine coverage among evangelicals became even more accentuated after adjustment for covariates, including education and wealth, suggesting that the gap is not due to known confounding variables.
66.Rationale: The passage explicitly documents that evangelicals have substantially lower COVID-19 vaccine coverage and that this disparity increases after adjustment for socioeconomic and demographic covariates, implying those factors do not explain the gap. The text links evangelical affiliation to political and anti-vaccine messaging (Bolsonaro), pointing to trust and messaging as likely drivers. Thus evangelical individuals are the group whose distribution most strongly supports the conclusion that public health messaging and trust, rather than individual clinical risk, shape uptake.

66.Option: Individuals in the lowest wealth quintile, who are at higher clinical risk due to comorbidities, show lower vaccine uptake, suggesting that socioeconomic disadvantage drives vaccine hesitancy more than public health messaging
Evidence: A positive socioeconomic gradient was observed for COVID-19 coverage with a gap of 9.4 pp among the top and bottom quintiles, but no significant differences were observed in influenza vaccine coverage ( P = 0.468).

The positive gradient with schooling was attenuated in the wealth-adjusted analyses but remained significant. A positive wealth gradient existed for COVID-19 vaccination, which was no longer stepwise or significant in the adjusted model that included schooling as a covariate.
In spite of the collinearity between the two explanatory variables, our results suggest that education is a stronger determinant of vaccine coverage than wealth.
66.Rationale: The passage reports a wealth gradient, but also states that the association becomes non-stepwise/non-significant after adjusting for schooling and that education appears a stronger determinant than wealth. Moreover, the evangelical finding (persisting after adjustment) highlights messaging/trust effects that are not explained by socioeconomic disadvantage. Therefore the option's claim that socioeconomic disadvantage rather than messaging is the primary driver is not supported by the presented analyses.

67.Option: Application of a hierarchical nomenclature system to group isolates by serotype and allele code for temporal trend analysis
Evidence: By applying tree-temporal scan statistics prospectively to genomic surveillance data with a standardized hierarchical nomenclature, we automatically sifted through large quantities of data in minutes and generated weekly ranked shortlists of nodes with statistically unusual numbers of recent cases.

We designated ‘SAL’ as the tree root and each Salmonella serotype (e.g. Typhi, Enteritidis, Kottbus) as the second tree level. We appended the allele code, which can be up to six digits, to the serotype.
This method flexibly evaluates all candidate clusters, across many degrees of genetic relatedness and date ranges.
67.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that the tree-temporal scan was applied to genomic data 'with a standardized hierarchical nomenclature' and that this approach 'flexibly evaluates ... across many degrees of genetic relatedness.' Using serotype + allele-code hierarchy lets the method consider clusters at multiple levels of genetic resolution (broad serotypes down to fine allele-code nodes), which enables detection of emerging clusters even when genetic relatedness is subtle because the scan can evaluate both broad and narrow groupings rather than relying on a single fixed grouping.

67.Option: Use of a rolling 365-day period to detect persistent increases in case counts across all Salmonella serotypes
Evidence: Weekly, starting on 16 November 2022, we downloaded from SEDRIC the allele codes for salmonellosis (typhoidal and non-typhoidal) for New York State residents, as additional parsing of patient addresses was necessary to restrict to NYC residents. We determined counts of each Salmonella allele code among NYC residents during a rolling 365-day period, ending on the most recent specimen collection date ( Table 1 ).
This method flexibly evaluates all candidate clusters, across many degrees of genetic relatedness and date ranges.
67.Rationale: Although the authors used a rolling 365-day window for Salmonella counts, the question asks which feature of the analytical method enables detection when genetic relatedness is subtle and temporal clustering is weak. The rolling-year window is a temporal framing choice that can detect persistent increases, but the passage attributes the ability to detect subtle genetic signals and weak temporal clustering to the TreeScan approach itself (evaluating many nodes/degrees of relatedness and temporal windows). Therefore the rolling 365-day window is a data-windowing detail, not the core methodological feature that allows detection under subtle/weak clustering conditions.

67.Option: Detection of statistical anomalies in case counts over time across the phylogenetic tree
Evidence: We conducted prospective analyses by using tree-temporal scan statistics ... We searched for unusual increases that emerged over any recent time period at any node, from large phylogenetic branches to small groups of genetically indistinguishable isolates.
TreeScan detects statistical anomalies, which must be investigated to distinguish true clusters from data-quality issues.

Under the null hypothesis, for each variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is constant over time. Under the alternative hypothesis, for one variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is higher during some recent period.
67.Rationale: The passage describes TreeScan as searching for 'unusual increases' (statistical anomalies) at any node of the phylogenetic tree and explicitly states that TreeScan 'detects statistical anomalies.' This node-by-time anomaly detection across the tree (many levels of relatedness) is the feature that enables detection even when genetic relatedness is subtle and temporal clustering is weak because it does not require strong, obvious genetic or temporal clustering to flag an unusual deviation from baseline proportions.

67.Option: Identification of genetically indistinguishable isolates through high-resolution allele code matching at the sixth digit
Evidence: We searched for unusual increases that emerged over any recent time period at any node, from large phylogenetic branches to small groups of genetically indistinguishable isolates.
Isolates with more allele code digits in common have a lower number of allele differences ( Table 3 ).

For Salmonella , the signal-to-noise ratio to detect a new cluster was poor for allele codes that ended in ‘x’, as the underlying four-, five-, and six-digit codes were masked due to low genomic diversity that increased the within-code distance beyond the assignment thresholds.
67.Rationale: While the method can detect clusters of genetically indistinguishable isolates and allele-code digits represent resolution, the option focuses narrowly on 'sixth digit matching' as the enabling feature. The passage indicates the scan works across many levels of genetic resolution (not only exact sixth-digit matches) and also notes limitations at very fine-grained masked codes. The key enabling feature for detecting clusters when relatedness is subtle or temporal clustering weak is the tree-temporal scan's ability to evaluate many nodes and find statistical anomalies, not solely identification of perfectly indistinguishable isolates at the sixth-digit allele code.

67.Option: Comparison of observed case counts to expected counts derived from baseline proportions across all detected nodes
Evidence: Under the null hypothesis, for each variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is constant over time. Under the alternative hypothesis, for one variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is higher during some recent period.

For example, if a node has 5.4% of cases during the baseline period (i.e. prior to the cluster period) and there are 100 total cases with WGS results during the cluster period, then the expected number of cases during the cluster period at that node is 5.4.
For each node (candidate cluster), a likelihood ratio-based test statistic is calculated when the observed number of cases during the time window at the node exceeds the expected number.
67.Rationale: The passage describes that TreeScan computes expected counts from baseline proportions for each node and compares observed vs expected counts using a likelihood-ratio test. This node-wise observed-versus-expected comparison is central to identifying unusual increases (clusters) even when absolute genetic similarity or tight temporal clustering is limited, because it flags nodes with higher-than-expected recent representation relative to their baseline proportion.

68.Option: The temporal lag between preprint posting and peer-reviewed publication may introduce reverse causality, where public attention drives citation counts rather than the other way around
Evidence: Preprints were also widely reported and shared: medRxiv received >10 million monthly page views at the pandemic peak [ 6 ], with significant implications for public health messaging [ 7 ].

For COVID-19 papers, there was greater alignment between scientific interest and public attention. It may be that papers with intrinsic scientific merit gained more attention, were more highly cited, and were more likely to be published in higher-impact-factor journals. Conversely, media and social media attention could have increased a paper’s chances of being cited or published in higher-impact journals, especially for COVID-19 papers.
Previous research has framed Altmetrics impact as being ‘predictive’ of higher citations [ 21 ] but causality has not been investigated and cannot be inferred from this analysis.
68.Rationale: The passage explicitly notes that media/social attention could increase a paper’s chance of being cited and that causality cannot be inferred. Because preprints are posted earlier than peer-reviewed publications and received large public attention, this temporal ordering can plausibly create reverse causality: high Altmetrics shortly after preprinting could drive later citation accrual rather than citations driving Altmetrics. The quoted sentences directly support the plausibility of this mechanism.

68.Option: Incomplete data linkage and coverage may introduce measurement bias, leading to an inaccurate estimate of the true correlation between scientific and public attention
Evidence: Linkage of preprints to subsequent peer-reviewed publications may be incomplete, resulting in biased estimates of publication rates and predictors of publication.
Granular Altmetrics data were not available for all papers owing to computational limitations.
The Dimensions dataset, while extensive, does not capture 100% of the research literature.
68.Rationale: The passage explicitly lists incomplete linkage and incomplete Altmetrics/journal coverage as limitations that can bias estimates. Missing or mislinked records and incomplete Altmetrics capture would directly distort measured citation counts, Altmetrics scores, or the pairing between them, producing a discrepancy between the observed correlation and the true underlying association.

68.Option: Differences in citation practices across disciplines may distort the correlation between scientific attention and public interest, especially when comparing studies on highly publicized topics like COVID-19 with those on less visible topics
Evidence: citation-based metrics of scientific attention and scientific visibility were citation count (at the time of data export, March 2023); citation rate (citation count/days since publication); field citation ratio (citations normalized to the field of research and publication date of the paper); and Journal Citation Ratio (JCR—a field-normalized version of the IF).
For COVID-19 journal articles, we observed a much stronger correlation between citation metrics and the Altmetrics score than for non-COVID-19 articles or pre-pandemic articles ( Figure 4A ).
68.Rationale: While discipline-specific citation practices can in general distort citation-based comparisons, the study explicitly used field-normalized metrics (field citation ratio, JCR) to mitigate such distortions. Because the authors accounted for field differences in their metrics, differential citation practices across disciplines are less likely to be the primary explanation for a discrepancy between observed and true associations in this analysis. The passage therefore does not support this option as the most plausible explanation.

68.Option: The high volume of preprints during the pandemic may have led to a dilution of scientific attention, causing a spurious reduction in the correlation between citations and Altmetrics scores
Evidence: Demand for rapid publication led to a substantial surge in preprint usage: medRxiv submissions increased 10-fold between January and May 2020 [ 6 ].
COVID-19 preprints spiked to a high of >4000/month in May 2020 but declined steadily over the remainder of the study period ( Figure 2B ).

The distribution of citations is highly skewed: a majority of papers received few or no citations and a small minority received a very large number ( Supplementary Figure S3 ). The skew is more pronounced in COVID-19 papers and preprints: 2.6% of COVID-19 papers had received ≥100 citations vs 0.2% of non-COVID-19 papers during the same period ( Supplementary Figure S3 and Table 1 ).
68.Rationale: Although the passage documents a large increase in preprint volume and a highly skewed distribution of citations, it does not present evidence that a 'dilution' effect reduced the correlation between citations and Altmetrics. In fact, the authors observed stronger correlations between citation metrics and Altmetrics for COVID-19 journal articles and preprints. Therefore, while volume and skew could theoretically influence correlations, the text does not support the specific claim that high preprint volume caused a spurious reduction in the citation–Altmetrics correlation in this study.

69.Option: The association between ferritin and CKD may reflect the cumulative burden of metabolic risk factors such as obesity and diabetes, which are more prevalent in urban and migrant populations
Evidence: Compared with the 1276 without CKD, cases were older (50±1 vs 45±1 years), more often female, and had higher body mass index (BMI), waist–hip ratios, and prevalences of hypertension (50.9% vs 36.1%) and diabetes (11.3% vs 5.7%).
Models were adjusted for demographics, lifestyle, anthropometrics, and medication use.
A 1-SD increase in ferritin was associated with a higher risk of incident CKD (aIRR: 3.53, 95% CI: 2.42–5.01) and albuminuria (aIRR: 4.22, 95% CI: 2.87–6.10)
69.Rationale: Although metabolic risk factors (obesity, diabetes) are more common among CKD cases, the analysis reporting the ferritin–CKD association adjusted for demographics, lifestyle, anthropometrics and medications. The strong adjusted association (aIRR 3.53) therefore cannot be simply attributed to confounding by measured metabolic risk factors. The passage therefore does not support interpreting the ferritin–CKD link as merely a reflection of metabolic burden in urban/migrant groups.

69.Option: Ferritin levels may be elevated due to acute infections during follow-up, which could have caused transient inflammation and contributed to CKD development, explaining the observed association
Evidence: We excluded 409 individuals with symptoms of acute infection (fever, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, runny nose); those receiving treatment for TB, HIV, or hepatitis C; and those on systemic antibacterial, antifungal, corticosteroid, or antiviral medications.
Participants on treatment for chronic infectious diseases (e.g. HIV, TB) were excluded. However, undiagnosed or untreated chronic infections could still have influenced the biomarker levels.

To better determine whether ferritin can reliably predict CKD risk, it is crucial to conduct detailed studies with multiple ferritin measurements, as well as information on acute infection and hemoglobin over time in relation to eGFR and albuminuria
69.Rationale: Acute infections were screened for and symptomatic individuals were excluded at baseline, and the authors note the need for repeated ferritin and infection data over time. While acute infections during follow-up could in theory transiently raise ferritin, the study lacks repeated measures to confirm this; the authors emphasize that undiagnosed or chronic infections (not transient acute events during follow-up) could influence ferritin. Thus the passage does not support acute intercurrent infections during follow-up as the primary explanation for the observed prospective association.

69.Option: Elevated ferritin levels may indicate iron overload, which directly damages renal tubules through oxidative stress, independent of inflammation, explaining its association with CKD incidence
Evidence: Ferritin serves as both an inflammatory marker and an indicator of iron storage.
It is possible that elevated ferritin, as a marker of iron overload, may contribute to kidney damage through mechanisms involving oxidative stress and inflammation

When ferritin was categorized by iron status (deficiency, normal, overload), no associations were observed with CKD incidence, albuminuria, or eGFR, although a trend was noted toward higher albuminuria and lower eGFR in those with iron overload ( Supplementary Table 4 ).
69.Rationale: The passage explicitly acknowledges iron overload as a plausible mechanism (oxidative stress) but frames ferritin as both an inflammation marker and an iron-storage marker; the authors describe oxidative stress acting together with inflammation rather than ferritin causing damage entirely independent of inflammation. Moreover, categorical iron-status analyses did not show clear associations (only trends). Therefore the claim that the ferritin–CKD link is explained solely by iron-overload tubular damage independent of inflammation is not supported by the data or the authors' interpretation.

69.Option: Elevated ferritin levels likely reflect cumulative infection-driven inflammation rather than metabolic inflammation, explaining its stronger association with CKD incidence in this population
Evidence: Given the high prevalence of both acute and chronic infections, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, and malaria, in the SSA region, there is growing evidence that these infections contribute to renal injury and increase the risk of CKD.
Ferritin serves as both an inflammatory marker and an indicator of iron storage.
This finding ... supports the role of ferritin as a marker of chronic inflammation in this population.
The z-standardized CRP levels were not associated with incident CKD ...

The absence of an observed association in our cohort may suggest an alternative mechanism such as inflammatory adaptation. In populations with prolonged exposure to infectious or environmental antigens, the immune system may recalibrate to a higher CRP 'set point' without causing proportional tissue injury.
69.Rationale: The passage emphasizes a high burden of chronic infections in the study population and explicitly interprets ferritin as reflecting chronic inflammation in this context. CRP (often reflecting metabolic/low-grade inflammation) showed no association, and the authors propose immune adaptation that could make CRP less informative. Taken together, the most supported interpretation is that elevated ferritin captures cumulative infection-driven (chronic) inflammatory processes relevant to CKD risk in this population.

69.Option: The lack of association between CRP and CKD suggests that chronic inflammation is not a driver of CKD in this population, and ferritin is a more reliable marker of systemic inflammation
Evidence: The z-standardized CRP levels were not associated with incident CKD based on KDIGO criteria [adjusted IRR (aIRR): 1.02, 95% CI: 0.84–1.15]
Ferritin serves as both an inflammatory marker and an indicator of iron storage.
This finding ... supports the role of ferritin as a marker of chronic inflammation in this population.

The absence of an observed association in our cohort may suggest an alternative mechanism such as inflammatory adaptation. In populations with prolonged exposure to infectious or environmental antigens, the immune system may recalibrate to a higher CRP 'set point' without causing proportional tissue injury.
69.Rationale: While CRP was not associated with CKD, the authors do not conclude that chronic inflammation is not a driver of CKD. Instead, they propose that CRP may be an insensitive indicator in this setting (inflammatory adaptation) and that ferritin may better capture chronic inflammation or iron-related mechanisms. Thus it is incorrect to infer from the CRP null that chronic inflammation is not involved; the passage supports the opposite interpretation: ferritin may be a more informative marker of the relevant (likely infection-driven) inflammatory processes.

70.Option: Increased behavioral risk-taking and reduced health literacy among young and middle-aged male Medical Aid beneficiaries
Evidence: low-income individuals are more prone to experiencing poor preexisting health conditions, as they are more likely to face barriers to the adoption of healthy behaviors and management of chronic health conditions due to financial constraints and limited social support networks [ 29 ].
The lack of fundamental social support and assistance increases the risk of adverse health outcomes, making disease detection and management challenging, and exacerbating existing health conditions.
70.Rationale: While the passage notes that low-income individuals face barriers to healthy behaviors and management of chronic conditions, it does not emphasize increased behavioral risk-taking or reduced health literacy as the primary explanation for the higher cold-related hospitalizations among young and middle-aged males. The authors specifically highlight occupational/outdoor exposure as the leading conjectured driver for this subgroup. Therefore, this option is not the most likely factor according to the passage.

70.Option: Higher occupational exposure to outdoor extreme temperatures due to employment in physically intensive industries such as construction and agriculture
Evidence: we cautiously conjectured that these results might have been related to occupational and outdoor activities in young and middle-aged populations.

In South Korea, economically disadvantaged males tend to work in relatively more intensive industries (such as construction, agriculture, and transportation) that can increase exposure to outdoor extreme temperatures, compared with females and males who are not socially marginalized [ 6 ].

Second, people who have outdoor jobs might be more frequently and intensively exposed to extreme temperatures for extended periods and, in general, this outdoor working group (included in blue-collar occupations) has relatively lower socioeconomic and health conditions compared with people with indoor working conditions [ 16 ].
70.Rationale: The passage directly attributes the higher vulnerability among young and middle-aged MA beneficiaries—especially males—to greater occupational and outdoor exposure. The authors explicitly conjecture occupational/outdoor activities as a likely explanation and provide examples of intensive industries (construction, agriculture, transportation) that increase cold exposure, making this the most likely explanation in the text.

70.Option: Higher prevalence of mental health disorders among young and middle-aged male Medical Aid beneficiaries leading to impaired temperature regulation
Evidence: MA beneficiaries experienced higher risks of mental disorders than those who were not eligible.

We suspect that the compounding effects of poverty-related stressors, such as financial insecurity and social isolation, can increase susceptibility to temperature-related mental health crises [ 38 ].
70.Rationale: The passage documents higher rates of mental-disorder–related ED admissions among MA beneficiaries and suggests poverty-related stressors increase susceptibility to temperature-related mental health crises. However, it does not describe impaired physiological temperature regulation due to mental disorders as the main mechanism for the observed pattern among young and middle-aged males. The authors instead point to occupational exposure as the leading explanation, so this option is not the most likely according to the passage.

70.Option: Greater susceptibility to cold due to preexisting health conditions exacerbated by financial constraints and limited access to healthcare
Evidence: low-income individuals are more prone to experiencing poor preexisting health conditions, as they are more likely to face barriers to the adoption of healthy behaviors and management of chronic health conditions due to financial constraints and limited social support networks [ 29 ].
The financial constraints also limit access to healthcare, delay treatment for temperature-related illnesses, and worsen health outcomes [ 17–19 ].
Therefore, as MA beneficiaries usually suffer from financial burdens, the study showed that they need to be protected from acute health events.
70.Rationale: The passage supports that poorer preexisting health and limited access to care increase vulnerability to temperature-related illness among MA beneficiaries generally. However, the question targets the specific pattern among young and middle-aged males; the authors attribute that age/sex pattern primarily to greater occupational outdoor exposure rather than to preexisting comorbidity or care access. Thus, while preexisting conditions plausibly contribute overall, they are not presented as the most likely primary explanation for the observed subgroup pattern.

70.Option: Greater reliance on alcohol for warmth during cold weather due to inability to afford heating, increasing cold-related health risks
Evidence: we observed a positive association between ED admissions for substance abuse disorders and cold temperatures among MA-eligible patients in contrast to the negative association that was observed in the non-eligible group ( Supplementary Table S8 ; see online supplementary material for a color version of this table).

economically marginalized individuals who lack the ability to heat their homes may resort to increased alcohol abuse to heat themselves [ 39 ]. Consequently, MA beneficiaries may be more likely to experience alcohol-related disorders, which worsen their overall mental health.
70.Rationale: The passage does present a plausible mechanism linking alcohol use to cold-related ED admissions among MA beneficiaries and provides evidence of substance-abuse–related admissions associated with cold. However, the authors emphasize occupational/outdoor exposure as the primary conjectured driver for the higher cold-related hospitalization risk in young and middle-aged males. Therefore, although alcohol reliance may contribute, the passage does not support it as the most likely primary explanation for that specific observed pattern.

71.Option: Adjust for central adiposity as a covariate in a Cox proportional hazards model to estimate the association between age at menarche and diabetes incidence
Evidence: We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age.

78.Rationale: Including area-level deprivation (a measured contextual covariate) will help reduce confounding from measurable area-level factors — the passage shows its exclusion materially changed estimates — but the question asks about confounding from unmeasured area-level characteristics. The text emphasizes that control for assessment centre (a proxy for geographic area) is particularly important to limit spatial confounding due to unobserved area-level characteristics. Thus, while including deprivation is useful, it does not most directly mitigate confounding from unmeasured area-level factors.

78.Option: Match cases and controls on residential location to eliminate variation in unmeasured area-level factors
Evidence: The analysis was based on a design strategy and model selection described in detail in previous work [11]. We applied a Cox proportional hazard model with time-varying exposures.

In our main (full) model, we used calendar time as the time axis, we stratified by indicators of sex, assessment centre, and year of birth, and finally, we adjusted directly for all the other covariates listed in the previous section.
78.Rationale: The study context described is a cohort/time-to-event analysis (Cox model with time-varying exposures), not a matched case–control design. Moreover, matching on location would remove between-area variation (which could be desirable) but is not the approach the authors recommend; instead they stress stratification or area-level modeling of assessment centre. Therefore matching cases and controls on residential location is not the most directly applicable choice in this repeated-observation cohort context.

Evidence: We conducted a sensitivity analysis for the inclusion of the assessment centre in the statistical model using different specifications, following a previous work [10]. Specifically, we used dummy variables or random effects with a gamma distribution or normal distribution.

78.Rationale: Applying random effects for assessment centre is an explicit hierarchical modeling strategy to account for unmeasured area-level heterogeneity (unobserved area-level characteristics). The passage reports that random-effects specifications (at least some distributions) gave results consistent with stratification and indicators, indicating that random effects are a viable approach to mitigate unmeasured spatial confounding. Thus this design/modeling choice directly targets unmeasured area-level confounding.

Evidence: Contextual features were represented by the assessment centre (as a proxy for residential location) ...

In our main (full) model, we used calendar time as the time axis, we stratified by indicators of sex, assessment centre, and year of birth, and finally, we adjusted directly for all the other covariates listed in the previous section.

First, control for assessment centre is important to limit spatial confounding, occurring primarily through the path involving unobserved area-level characteristics linked with differential outdoor PM2.5 levels.

79.Option: The increased risk of chronic bronchitis and eczema in offspring of fathers who used snus in puberty suggests that the vulnerability window is linked to respiratory and skin development processes
Evidence: After adjustment for paternal smoking and the offspring’s current smoking and other confounding factors, the offspring whose fathers started using snus in puberty had a higher risk of current allergic asthma [odds ratio (OR) 1.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.02–1.97], but not for non-allergic asthma. 79.Rationale: While the passage does report increased risks of chronic bronchitis and eczema among offspring of fathers who began snus use in puberty, the option asserts a specific link to 'respiratory and skin development processes' as the primary support for a developmental-window hypothesis. The stronger, more direct support for a puberty-window vulnerability in the paper is the contrast by timing of exposure (puberty vs after puberty). Observing higher risks for particular outcomes (chronic bronchitis, eczema) is consistent with an effect, but by itself does not most strongly demonstrate that a specific developmental window (puberty) is the critical driver; it could reflect outcome-specific susceptibility rather than timing per se. Therefore this option overstates what the outcome pattern alone most strongly supports.

They also had increased risk of ... chronic bronchitis ..., and eczema ... ( Fig. 3 and Table 3 ). These results imply that nicotine may exert long-lasting effects on respiratory health across generations in mammals, in accordance with our results for the offspring health effects of a father’s exposure to snus—a high-nicotine-content product.

Thus, novel studies suggest that perturbations to epigenetic material in germ cells occurring during vulnerable periods, including puberty, may be passed on and act as drivers of information through generations [ 10 ].
79.Rationale: The most direct evidence in the study for a puberty-specific vulnerability is the clear contrast by timing: fathers who began snus use in puberty had increased offspring risks, whereas fathers who began after puberty did not show consistent risk increases. This contrast (same exposure type but different timing) is precisely the pattern that supports a critical developmental window during puberty as the period of heightened vulnerability.

79.Option: The consistency of results across multiple sensitivity analyses, including exclusion of offspring who used snus themselves, strengthens the argument that the vulnerability window is due to inherited epigenetic changes
Evidence: Results were consistent after the exclusion of offspring (i) who reported snus use during their puberty ( n = 67) ( Table 4 and Supplementary Table 1 ), (ii) who used other nicotine-containing products ( n = 89; estimates not shown), (iii) whose fathers reported rhinitis ( n = 259) ( Table 4 and Supplementary Table 2 ), or (iv) whose mothers smoked in pregnancy ( n = 291) ( Supplementary Table 4 ).
Recent human epigenetic research has linked blood DNA methylation changes in offspring to father’s smoking initiation in puberty, partly associated with asthma and wheeze [ 13 ].
Suggested mechanisms explaining how early parental exposures influence future generations point to epigenetic programming.
79.Rationale: While the passage documents that results were robust across multiple sensitivity analyses (which reduces the likelihood that observed associations are due to measured confounding or offspring behavior), robustness alone does not prove the mechanism is inherited epigenetic change. The authors posit epigenetic programming as a plausible mechanism and cite supporting epigenetic studies, but sensitivity analysis consistency does not constitute direct evidence of epigenetic inheritance. Therefore the option's causal claim ('due to inherited epigenetic changes') is not warranted solely by the sensitivity analyses and so is incorrect.

79.Option: The higher odds ratios for chronic bronchitis and eczema compared to allergic asthma suggest that the vulnerability window is most pronounced for non-respiratory systems
Evidence: They also had increased risk of at least three asthma symptoms with allergy (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.10–1.21), chronic bronchitis (OR 2.17; 95% CI 1.04–4.54), and eczema (OR 1.45; 95%CI 1.27–1.65) ( Fig. 3 and Table 3 ).

After adjustment for paternal smoking and the offspring’s current smoking and other confounding factors, the offspring whose fathers started using snus in puberty had a higher risk of current allergic asthma [odds ratio (OR) 1.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.02–1.97], but not for non-allergic asthma.
79.Rationale: This option misinterprets the outcome domains. Chronic bronchitis is a respiratory condition, so an elevated OR for chronic bronchitis does not indicate that the vulnerability window is 'most pronounced for non-respiratory systems.' Moreover, the evidence shows increased risk for allergic asthma and eczema (an allergic/skin outcome), indicating effects across respiratory and allergic domains rather than being limited to non-respiratory systems. Thus the inference in the option is incorrect.

79.Option: The association between paternal snus use and offspring allergic asthma, but not non-allergic asthma, suggests that the developmental window of vulnerability is specific to immune-mediated pathways
Evidence: After adjustment for paternal smoking and the offspring’s current smoking and other confounding factors, the offspring whose fathers started using snus in puberty had a higher risk of current allergic asthma [odds ratio (OR) 1.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.02–1.97], but not for non-allergic asthma.

Recent human epigenetic research has linked blood DNA methylation changes in offspring to father’s smoking initiation in puberty, partly associated with asthma and wheeze [ 13 ].

Therefore this option is supported by the passage.

81.Option: CRP levels at age 9 years are associated with both ACEs and subsequent urinary incontinence, supporting a biological mechanism
Evidence: There was evidence that a higher ACE score was associated with a higher level of IL-6 (expressed as the percentage change in IL-6 per unit increase in ACE score) [1.03 (3%), 95% CI 1.01–1.05 (adjusted); Supplementary Table S8 ] but not CRP.

This aligns with the understanding that the etiological mechanisms of non-cardia GC and cardia GC are likely different [ 6 , 7 ].
82.Rationale: The passage directly states that cardia and non-cardia gastric cancers have different etiologies: obesity-related mechanisms (GERD and Barrett's esophagus) plausibly increase cardia cancer risk, whereas non-cardia cancer is linked to chronic gastritis and H. pylori. 82.Rationale: The passage reports similar percentages of overweight across cardia and non-cardia cases and controls, and the authors explored and addressed heterogeneity without finding that regional BMI distribution explained the differing associations. 83.Option: Including only DCIS cases diagnosed before any invasive breast cancer to ensure that each case is counted as a unique event in the incidence calculation
Evidence: When a DCIS is followed by an invasive BC with the same International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (ICD-O)-3 morphology code, only the invasive primary is retained in the ‘clean’ database in order to generate standard incidence statistics.
We excluded those patients with any of the following: history of invasive BC prior to DCIS diagnosis; simultaneous diagnosis of invasive BC and DCIS [ 7 ];
83.Rationale: Restricting to DCIS diagnosed before any invasive breast cancer (i.e., excluding those with prior invasive disease) is not the methodological choice that most directly addresses the specific misclassification problem described. The passage shows the registry’s standard (clean) database already drops DCIS when it is followed by an invasive BC, and the investigators explicitly excluded patients with a history of invasive BC prior to DCIS. However, the principal concern cited is under-ascertainment of DCIS because the clean database does not retain DCIS followed by later invasive BC. Merely including only DCIS cases diagnosed before any invasive disease would not correct that undercount; in fact it could perpetuate or worsen misclassification. The investigators instead used a different database to capture such cases (see evidence for Option 1).

Evidence: When a DCIS is followed by an invasive BC with the same International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (ICD-O)-3 morphology code, only the invasive primary is retained in the ‘clean’ database in order to generate standard incidence statistics.

Consequently, the study data were retrieved from the ‘service’ database, a specially configured additional system that is used for internal purposes and retains all types of information collected, including the notifications of DCIS followed by the notification of an invasive BC.

Using that service database is the methodological choice that most directly mitigates misclassification bias from excluding DCIS cases followed by invasive cancer.

Evidence: When a DCIS is followed by an invasive BC with the same International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (ICD-O)-3 morphology code, only the invasive primary is retained in the ‘clean’ database in order to generate standard incidence statistics.

Therefore this option does not reflect the methodological choice actually described and so is not the most directly supported answer.

83.Option: Restricting the analysis to DCIS cases diagnosed in the absence of any prior or subsequent breast cancer to eliminate potential confounding from disease progression
Evidence: We excluded those patients with any of the following: history of invasive BC prior to DCIS diagnosis; simultaneous diagnosis of invasive BC and DCIS [ 7 ];

Evidence: Consequently, the study data were retrieved from the ‘service’ database, a specially configured additional system that is used for internal purposes and retains all types of information collected, including the notifications of DCIS followed by the notification of an invasive BC.

Instead, the authors addressed under-registration/misclassification by using the service database that retains those notifications and by quality-assuring the data.
